\chapter{Courtesy Words}
\label{ch:te-courtesy}
\hlchaptermodality{51}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can be polite in Telugu beyond thank you --- gratitude, a good turn, respect, a blessing, a salutation --- and name the piece that two of those words share.}

Complete TE-C51-salutation and demonstrate the chapter promise.

\section[kṛtajñata]{\te{కృతజ్ఞత} (kṛtajñata) — gratitude}

\label{lesson:TE-C51-gratitude}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{veḷḷostānu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కృతజ్ఞత}}
\textbf{\te{కృతజ్ఞత}} (\emph{kṛtajñata}) — \textquotedblleft{}gratitude\textquotedblright{}.

\emph{kṛta}, \textquotedblleft{}done\textquotedblright{}, plus \emph{jña}, \textquotedblleft{}knowing\textquotedblright{}: knowing what was done for you. That is the whole of gratitude in two Sanskrit syllables, and Telugu took it entire.

Set it beside \te{ధన్యవాదములు}, the thank-you from the first pages of this book, which is \textquotedblleft{}utterances of 'worthy'\textquotedblright{}. One word thanks by calling the giver worthy. The other thanks by admitting the debt is remembered. They are not the same gesture, and Telugu keeps both.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A second word for thanks, with a different picture inside it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kṛtajñata}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kṛtajñata}, then \emph{dhanyavādamulu}, and say which one remembers a debt
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{కృతజ్ఞత} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}gratitude\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mēlu]{\te{మేలు} (mēlu) — a good turn, a benefit}

\label{lesson:TE-C51-favour}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kṛtajñata} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{మేలు}}
\textbf{\te{మేలు}} (\emph{mēlu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a good turn, a benefit\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, and short. \te{మేల్} meant \textquotedblleft{}above\textquotedblright{}; the good is what is above. From it Telugu draws \te{మేలు}, a benefit or a good turn done to someone, and also the plain comparative sense of \textquotedblleft{}better\textquotedblright{}.

So \emph{idi mēlu} says \textquotedblleft{}this one is higher\textquotedblright{} and lets the height do the judging --- which is what English does too, in \emph{superior}, without anyone noticing any more.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mēlu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{mēlu}, then \emph{manci}, and say which one is a thing done and which is a quality
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{మేలు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a good turn, a benefit\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gauravaṁ]{\te{గౌరవం} (gauravaṁ) — respect}

\label{lesson:TE-C51-respect}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mēlu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{గౌరవం}}
\textbf{\te{గౌరవం}} (\emph{gauravaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}respect\textquotedblright{}.

\emph{gaurava} is the abstract noun of \emph{guru} --- the very word met one chapter ago as the teacher. Respect is weightiness: to hold someone in \te{గౌరవం} is to grant that what they say has mass.

Telugu marks the same idea in its grammar as well as its vocabulary. \te{మీరు} rather than \te{నువ్వు}, and the \textbf{-\te{అండి}} hung on the end of a verb, are \te{గౌరవం} turned into endings. A language can be polite in its words or in its shapes, and this one does both.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and one of them is a word you already knew wearing a different suit.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gauravaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{gauravaṁ}, then \emph{guruvu}, and name the syllable they share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{గౌరవం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}respect\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āśīrvādaṁ]{\te{ఆశీర్వాదం} (āśīrvādaṁ) — a blessing}

\label{lesson:TE-C51-blessing}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{gauravaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ఆశీర్వాదం}}
\textbf{\te{ఆశీర్వాదం}} (\emph{āśīrvādaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a blessing\textquotedblright{}.

\emph{āśīs}, a wish or a prayer, plus \emph{vāda}, an utterance: a blessing is a wish said out loud.

The ceremony behind it is still in daily use. You bend and touch an elder's feet, and what comes back is \te{ఆశీర్వాదం} --- a hand on the head --- at a birthday, before an examination, at a wedding, and at every departure.

Notice \emph{vāda} sitting there. It is the same piece inside \te{ధన్యవాదములు}, \textquotedblleft{}utterances of 'worthy'\textquotedblright{}. Twice now this language has counted a thing said as a thing given.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four courtesy words, and two of them are utterances by name.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āśīrvādaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{āśīrvādaṁ}, then \emph{dhanyavādamulu}, and name the piece they share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{ఆశీర్వాదం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a blessing\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[daṇḍaṁ]{\te{దండం} (daṇḍaṁ) — a salutation, \textquotedblleft{}my respects\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:TE-C51-salutation}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{āśīrvādaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{దండం}}
\textbf{\te{దండం}} (\emph{daṇḍaṁ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a salutation, \textquotedblleft{}my respects\textquotedblright{}\textquotedblright{}.

\te{దండం} is what you say with the palms together --- my respects --- offered to an elder, a temple, a photograph on the wall. Children are taught to say it long before anyone explains it.

Sanskrit \emph{daṇḍa} is a staff, a stick. The full form of the gesture, \emph{daṇḍa-praṇāma}, is the prostration where the body lies down straight as a staff. Telugu kept the word and let the body straighten most of the way up.

Hold on to \te{దండ}; it comes back in the next chapter carrying flowers.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five courtesy words: \te{కృతజ్ఞత}, \te{మేలు}, \te{గౌరవం}, \te{ఆశీర్వాదం}, \te{దండం}. Thanks, a good turn, respect, a blessing, and the greeting you make with your hands.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{daṇḍaṁ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{daṇḍaṁ}, then \emph{namaskāraṁ}, and say which one you would give a grandparent
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{దండం} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a salutation, \textquotedblleft{}my respects\textquotedblright{}\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
